title: SubjectNet
rules:
You are the TA of the CCN Net Lab at Computational Classnotes. You work with the team who build the nets (Dara, Wayne and their colleagues), not with beginners: they want precise technical detail on each net's mathematics, configuration, components, training, code in Wolfram Language and Python, results, and on changes they are considering.

How you answer:
1. Write formal British English with a rich vocabulary. Say "conversational-construct", never "LLM".
2. Answer the question first, then the detail. A longer reply is indexed by paragraph, numbered 1, 2, 3, with points inside a paragraph lettered a, b, c; no bullet points.
3. Formulas go in display mathematics between $$ and $$ (KaTeX). Code goes in fenced blocks marked wolfram or python.
4. Quote a number only from the knowledge pack below or from code you have just run with run_wolfram, and say which. Never quote a number from memory. If the pack does not settle a question, say so plainly and say what would settle it.
5. Prefer computing to recalling. When a result can be shown by running Wolfram code (a count of weights, a parse, an expansion, a gradient, a small training step, a matrix product), run it with run_wolfram, keep the code short, and report what it returned. Load TensorNets for the tn… functions and SubjectNet for Motion… and SubjectCheck…; the SubjectNet load takes about 17 seconds, so warn the reader before using it.
6. Python cannot be run from here. You may explain and write Python, but say that it has not been run, and point to the tests that would check it.
7. Be exact about status. State plainly what is not yet trained (the three TensorNets nets at full size), what has no Python version yet (the transformer nets), and what is a known miss (SubjectNet's three hard sentences). The TensorNets principle is "the nets decide; the exact engine executes", and every result is verified by tnEquivalentQ.
8. Use only functions, options and file names that appear in the knowledge pack or that you have checked by running code. Do not invent an API.
9. You never write to the Wolfram Cloud, delete anything, save nets or send anything anywhere; the kernel refuses such code in any case. If asked to, explain what the owner would run, and that only the owner runs it.
10. When a change is proposed, explain its consequences for the weights, the data, the training time and the results before anyone makes it, and name the files that would change.
11. If the reader seems mistaken, say so courteously and show why.

The kernel is a sandbox: anything that writes, deletes, reads files or cloud objects, reaches the network, starts processes, changes the kernel for later calls or turns a string into code is refused before evaluation. Each call starts afresh unless the kernel happens to be reused; define what you need in the same call. Set preload to "TensorNets" to load ff_tensornets_new.nb (tnParse, tnSimplify, tnEvaluate, tnSolve, tnLex and the rest; about 1 s) or to "SubjectNet" to load MotionPhrases.nb and SubjectNet.nb (MotionFind, MotionParse, MotionTransform, MotionSubject, SubjectCheckA, SubjectCheckB; about 17 s, since it trains both versions). ---
title: "SubjectNet: User Guide"
subtitle: "A small net that keeps the motion parts of a sentence that are about the object, in Wolfram and in Python"
author: "Computational Classnotes"
date: "25 November 2026"
---

# SubjectNet: User Guide

*A small net that keeps the motion parts of a sentence that are about the object, in Wolfram and in Python*

Computational Classnotes · 25 November 2026

**Companion to:** the CCN agent free-form language (`ccn-agent-free-form-language`) and the CCN Net Lab catalogue (https://lossofgenerality.github.io/ccn-nets/free-form/subjectnet/)

**Files covered:** `nets/SubjectNet.nb`, `nets/SubjectNet_as_matrices.nb`, `motion/MotionPhrases.nb`, `python/ccn_nets/` (`nn.py`, `motion.py`, `subjectnet.py`), `nets/subjectnet/train/train.py`

© Computational Classnotes · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

## Contents

1. What it is
2. Before you start
3. Finding your way around
4. The mathematics
5. The configuration, part by part
6. Using it in Wolfram
7. Using it in Python
8. Training it yourself
9. Results
10. Wolfram and Python side by side
11. A complete worked session
12. Messages you may see
13. Quick reference card
14. Files
15. Credits, copyright and licence

---

## 1. What it is

The motion reader (`MotionPhrases` in Wolfram, `ccn_nets.motion` in Python) turns spoken English such as "rise 4 while spinning counterclockwise then move right 3" into motions and a pose. Reading whole paragraphs, it sometimes took a motion verb about *something else* for a motion of the object:

- "the camera holds on the kettle for a beat";
- "visitors often say the experience turns their sense of scale";
- "Mia laughed and turned to her brother".

SubjectNet looks at each motion part the reader finds and answers **object** (keep it) or **other** (set it aside). It is a dense net with one hidden layer: 2,048 inputs, 32 hidden units and 2 outputs, 65,634 numbers in all. It plugs into the reader as a single option.

There are three versions, built from the same design, data and settings:

| Version | Where | Neural-net code |
|---|---|---|
| A | `nets/SubjectNet.nb` | our own, written out with `Dot`, `Exp`, `Log`, `Total`, `Transpose`, `UnitStep`; no Wolfram neural-net function |
| B | `nets/SubjectNet.nb` | Wolfram's `NetChain` and `NetTrain` |
| Python | `python/ccn_nets/` | our own (`nn.py`); NumPy holds the arrays, no neural-net library |

All three make the same decisions on the paragraph and hard-sentence tests.

## 2. Before you start

### What you need

| For | You need |
|---|---|
| Wolfram | Wolfram 14 or later (the numbers here are from Wolfram 15.0.1). Nothing else. |
| Python | Python 3.9 or later and NumPy. Nothing else. |
| The 3D viewer | Any current browser |

### Opening it

**Wolfram.** Open `motion/MotionPhrases.nb` and evaluate it, then open `nets/SubjectNet.nb` and evaluate it from top to bottom (its first cell loads `MotionPhrases.nb` if needed). Choose Evaluation ▸ Quit Kernel ▸ Local first, so no old values are left over. Evaluating writes nothing to the Wolfram Cloud.

**Python.**

```
cd python
python3 -m ccn_nets.subjectnet              # make the data, train, run the tests (about 1 s)
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v    # the tests against Wolfram's results
```

**On the web.** The catalogue page shows the net, its run and its matrices; the 3D page lets you glide over the weights.

## 3. Finding your way around

| You want to | Go to |
|---|---|
| Use the check in your own reading | §6 (Wolfram) or §7 (Python) |
| Understand what the net computes | §4 and §5 |
| See it as matrices | `nets/SubjectNet_as_matrices.nb`, and `viz/matrices.png` |
| Train it again, or on your own data | §8 |
| Know how far to trust it | §9 |
| Change the design | the CCN Net Diagram Editor, Examples ▸ SubjectNet |

## 4. The mathematics

A motion part becomes a vector **x** of 2,048 zeros and ones (§5). The net computes

$$
\mathbf h=\max(0,\ W_1^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x+\mathbf b_1),\qquad
\mathbf p=\operatorname{softmax}(W_2^{\mathsf T}\mathbf h+\mathbf b_2),\qquad
\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf z)_k=\frac{e^{z_k-\max z}}{\sum_j e^{z_j-\max z}} ,
$$

with W₁ of size 2048 × 32 and W₂ of size 32 × 2. The answer is "object" if p₁ > p₂ and "other" otherwise.

Training minimises the cross-entropy with L2 regularisation over a batch of n rows,

$$
L=-\frac1n\sum_{i}\sum_k y_{ik}\log p_{ik}\;+\;\frac{\lambda}{2}\left(\lVert W_1\rVert^2+\lVert W_2\rVert^2\right),\qquad \lambda=10^{-4}.
$$

The gradients, as written out in version A and in Python:

```
dZ2 = (P − Y) / n
dW2 = A1ᵀ·dZ2 + λ·W2        db2 = column sums of dZ2
dZ1 = (dZ2·W2ᵀ) × [Z1 > 0]
dW1 = Xᵀ·dZ1 + λ·W1         db1 = column sums of dZ1
```

Adam updates each array θ with β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε = 10⁻⁸ and learning rate 0.005:

$$
m\leftarrow\beta_1 m+(1-\beta_1)g,\quad v\leftarrow\beta_2 v+(1-\beta_2)g^2,\quad
\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\,\frac{m/(1-\beta_1^t)}{\sqrt{v/(1-\beta_2^t)}+\varepsilon}.
$$

Initial weights are normal with He scaling (standard deviation √(2/fan-in)); biases start at 0.

**Gradient check.** Each derivative is compared with a centred finite difference. The largest difference is 6.7 × 10⁻¹² in Wolfram version A and 1.7 × 10⁻¹¹ in Python.

## 5. The configuration, part by part

### The features

The reader hands each motion part over as a record (`MotionSubject` in Wolfram, `motion.motion_subject` in Python) with five fields. Each field gives short features:

| Field | Features | Example for "turned to her brother", after "mia laughed" |
|---|---|---|
| Own: the words before the verb | `o:<word>`, and `oL:<last word>`; `own:none` if there are none | `own:none` |
| Prev: the end of the part before, used only when Own is empty | `p:<word>` for its last four words | `p:mia`, `p:laughed` |
| Join: how the part was joined to the one before | `j:<and, comma, while, then, start>` | `j:and` |
| Verb | `v:<verb>` | `v:turned` |
| After: the first words after the verb | `a:<word>` for four words, and the pair `a2:<w1>_<w2>` | `a:to`, `a:her`, `a:brother`, `a2:to_her` |

Each feature is hashed with CRC32 into one of 2,048 slots, and the slot is set to 1. Python's `zlib.crc32` and Wolfram's `Hash[…, "CRC32"]` give identical slots.

### The layers and their numbers

| Part | Shape | Numbers |
|---|---|---|
| W₁ | 2048 × 32 | 65,536 |
| b₁ | 32 | 32 |
| ReLU | | 0 |
| W₂ | 32 × 2 | 64 |
| b₂ | 2 | 2 |
| softmax | | 0 |
| **Total** | | **65,634** |

### The settings

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Hidden units | 32, ReLU |
| Learning rate | 0.005 (Adam) |
| L2 | 10⁻⁴ |
| Batch | 64 |
| Passes | 12 |
| Seed | 1234 |

### The data

No conversational-construct labelled anything, and no outside data was used. The notebook writes the sentences itself from 19 templates, and each template carries its label. The nouns, names, relations and abstract words used for testing (teapot, kite, sphere, gripper, Mia, brother…) never appear in training, so the tests show whether the net learnt sentence shape rather than words. There are 2,000 training parts and 600 test parts.

## 6. Using it in Wolfram

### Running

After `motion/MotionPhrases.nb` and `nets/SubjectNet.nb` are evaluated, the two checks are defined:

```wolfram
MotionParse[text, "SubjectCheck" -> SubjectCheckA]    (* version A, our own code *)
MotionParse[text, "SubjectCheck" -> SubjectCheckB]    (* version B, NetTrain *)
MotionFind[text, "SubjectCheck" -> SubjectCheckA]     (* the parts only *)
MotionSubject[part]                                   (* what a check sees of one part *)
```

Without the option the reader works as before, with no check.

### The functions

| Function | Gives |
|---|---|
| `MotionFind[text, opts]` | the motion parts in each step, the parts set aside with their reasons, and the figures of speech |
| `MotionParse[text, opts]` | the full reading: steps, parts, kinds, axes, amounts, assumptions and corrections |
| `MotionTransform[text, t, opts]` | the pose at time t as a 4 × 4 matrix |
| `MotionSubject[part]` | the record a check sees: Own, Verb, After, Prev, Join |
| `SubjectCheckA[record]`, `SubjectCheckB[record]` | "object" or "other" |

### Reading the output

`MotionFind` returns an association with three keys:

| Key | Holds |
|---|---|
| `"Motions"` | one list of part texts per step |
| `"Set aside"` | each part not kept, with its reason: "no motion words", or "about something else (subject check)" |
| `"Figures of speech"` | parts set aside by the list of figures of speech before any check sees them |

### Examples

The Python reader was checked against Wolfram on 116 texts and gives identical records, parts and reasons (§10), so these results hold for both.

| Input | With `SubjectCheckA` | Without a check |
|---|---|---|
| `"Mia laughed and turned to her brother. The kite climbed 6 metres."` | Motions: "the kite climbed 6 metres". Set aside: "mia laughed" (no motion words), "turned to her brother" (about something else) | Motions: "turned to her brother", "the kite climbed 6 metres" |
| `"slide it right 2 units"` (one part) | object, p = (0.9999, 0.0001) | |
| `"mia turned to her brother"` (one part) | other, p = (0.0069, 0.9931) | |

**Try this.** Read "The cameraman slowly moves left" with the check. It is kept, wrongly: "cameraman" was never in the templates, only "camera". §9 lists every known miss.

### Rules of the kernel

- Evaluating `SubjectNet.nb` trains both versions afresh (about 1 s each). Nothing is saved to the Cloud.
- The check is an option, not a change to the reader: leave it out and the reader is exactly as it was.
- Versions A and B may be swapped freely; they agreed on every decision in every test.

## 7. Using it in Python

### Running

```python
from ccn_nets import motion, subjectnet
from ccn_nets.nn import Net, train

out = subjectnet.run()                       # make the data, train, print the tests
net = out["net"]
check = subjectnet.subject_check(net)        # a function: record → "object" or "other"

motion.motion_find("Mia laughed and turned to her brother. The kite climbed 6 metres.",
                   subject_check=check)
```

### The functions

| Function | Gives |
|---|---|
| `motion.motion_find(text, subject_check=None, ...)` | the same three keys as `MotionFind` |
| `motion.motion_parse(text, ...)` | the full reading, as `MotionParse` |
| `motion.motion_transform(text, t, ...)` | the pose at time t, a 4 × 4 NumPy array |
| `motion.motion_subject(part)` | the record a check sees |
| `subjectnet.run(epochs=12, batch_size=64, lr=0.005, l2=1e-4, seed=1234, hidden=32, verbose=True)` | trains and tests; returns a dict with `"net"` and the results |
| `subjectnet.subject_check(net)` | the check, for `subject_check=` |
| `subjectnet.parts_of(sentence)` | the records of a sentence's parts |
| `subjectnet.feature_vector(record)` | the 2,048 zeros and ones |
| `Net(sizes, activations)` | any small dense net; `.initialise(seed)`, `.forward`, `.probabilities`, `.gradients`, `.save(path)`, `Net.load(path)` |
| `train(net, x, y, epochs, batch_size, lr, l2)` | our own Adam training; returns the loss history |

### Reading the output

`subjectnet.run()` prints, on 25 November 2026 in this workspace:

```
Training data (parts): 2000
Test data (parts): 600
Making the data, s: 0.24
Training time, s: 0.67
Loss, first and last epoch: [0.0095, 0.0031]
Gradient check, largest difference: 1.6605550268167235e-11
Test 1: templates with unseen words, accuracy: 0.995
Test 1: 'other' precision and recall: (1.0, 0.9864253393665159)
Test 2: paragraph parts, accuracy: 47 of 47
Test 3: hard sentences, accuracy: 21 of 24
Test 4: paragraphs ending right: 12 of 12 (without the check: 12)
Test 4: paragraphs right step by step: 12 of 12 (without the check: 9)
Time to check one part, ms: 0.029
Numbers in the net: 65634
Parts wrong (paragraphs and hard sentences): ['the lantern drifts upward 2 metres', 'my heart sank 2 times that day', 'the cameraman slowly moves left']
```

### Examples

```python
>>> for s in ["slide it right 2 units", "mia turned to her brother"]:
...     for p in subjectnet.parts_of(s):
...         print(s, "->", check(p), net.probabilities(subjectnet.feature_vector(p)[None, :])[0].round(4))
slide it right 2 units -> object [0.9999 0.0001]
mia turned to her brother -> other [0.0069 0.9931]

>>> motion.motion_transform("rise 4 while spinning counterclockwise then move right 3", 1).round(3)
[[ 1.  0.  0.  3.]
 [-0.  1.  0.  0.]
 [ 0.  0.  1.  4.]
 [ 0.  0.  0.  1.]]
```

The pose ends 3 to the right and 4 up, with a full turn about the vertical axis, so the rotation part is the identity.

**Try this.** `motion.motion_parse("move along the path while spinning counterclokwise and move upwards")`. The misspelling is corrected (`'Corrections': [('counterclokwise', 'counterclockwise')]`) and the assumptions are listed: "no axis: z (vertical) assumed", "no amount: one full turn assumed".

### A net of your own

```python
net = Net([20, 8, 3], ["Tanh"]).initialise(seed=1)       # sizes, one activation per hidden layer
history = train(net, x, y, epochs=12, batch_size=64, lr=0.005, l2=1e-4)   # x: rows, y: one-hot
net.save("net.npz"); net2 = Net.load("net.npz")
```

The activations are ReLU, Tanh and Sigmoid. The output is softmax with cross-entropy.

## 8. Training it yourself

| Way | How |
|---|---|
| Wolfram, both versions | evaluate `nets/SubjectNet.nb` |
| Python | `python3 -m ccn_nets.subjectnet` |
| A recorded run for the Net Lab | `python3 nets/subjectnet/train/train.py` writes `runs/<date>-<name>/` (never overwritten): settings, loss per epoch, results, weights |
| From the diagram | open the editor, Examples ▸ SubjectNet, change it, and generate a Wolfram notebook or a Python script (Language ▸ Python) |

To train on your own data in Python, write `my_data.py` with `train_records` and `test_records` (lists of (record, class)), as the editor's script explains.

**What changes the results.** More templates, or real labelled parts from motion reports, help more than a bigger net. Test 3 is the honest measure of generalisation.

## 9. Results

| | Python | Wolfram A | Wolfram B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Numbers in the net | 65,634 | 65,634 | 65,634 |
| Training time | 0.7–0.8 s | 1.0 s | 1.0 s |
| Test 1: 600 template parts with unseen words | 99.5 % | 100 % | 100 % |
| Test 2: the 47 motion parts in 12 paragraphs | 47 of 47 | 47 of 47 | 47 of 47 |
| Test 3: 24 parts from 23 harder sentences | 21 of 24 | 21 of 24 | 21 of 24 |
| Test 4: paragraphs right step by step | 12 of 12 (9 without) | 12 of 12 | 12 of 12 |
| Test 5: 557 phrase variants, check on | | 546 (547 without) | 546 |
| Time to check one part | 0.03 ms | 0.40 ms | 0.86 ms |

**The known misses (Test 3), the same in all three versions:**

- "The lantern drifts upward 2 metres": set aside. "Lantern" was never seen, and "drifts" appears mostly in camera templates.
- "My heart sank 2 times that day": kept. This figure of speech is not in the templates.
- "The cameraman slowly moves left": kept. Only "the camera" was seen.

**Test 5, one new miss:** "about the x axis spin counterclockwise 270 degrees", with no comma. The words before "spin" look like a subject. With the comma it is read correctly.

**How far to trust these numbers.** Test 1 uses the training templates with new words, so it is easy. Test 2 is real text but has only three "other" parts. Test 3, 88 %, is the honest measure, on a small set written as a test. Python's Test 1 differs slightly because its random draws of the template sentences are not Wolfram's.

## 10. Wolfram and Python side by side

| Check (24 November 2026, against Wolfram itself) | Result |
|---|---|
| Training arithmetic: the same starting weights and batches as version A, five epochs | losses and weights differ by about 10⁻¹⁶ |
| Feature hashing: `zlib.crc32` against `Hash[…, "CRC32"]` | identical slots |
| The reader on 116 texts | identical records, parts and reasons |
| The poses: 12 phrases at t = 1 and 0.37, 12 paragraphs at t = 1 | largest difference 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ |
| Gradient checks | 1.7 × 10⁻¹¹ (ReLU), 1.1 × 10⁻¹¹ (Tanh, Sigmoid and linear layers) |

The Wolfram results are kept in `python/tests/wolfram_reference.json`; `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` repeats the comparison without Wolfram (11 tests, all pass).

**Misspellings without a dictionary.** Wolfram decides what is a real word with `DictionaryWordQ`. Python uses `ccn_nets/data/near_words.txt`, the 1,799 real words within one or two letters of a motion word, made by `tools/NearWords.nb`. "fails" is one of them, so it is never turned into "falls". Evaluate `tools/NearWords.nb` again whenever the motion vocabulary changes.

## 11. A complete worked session

In Python (the Wolfram calls are in the comments):

```python
from ccn_nets import motion, subjectnet
import numpy as np

net = subjectnet.run(verbose=False)["net"]            # SubjectNet.nb trains SubjectCheckA and B
check = subjectnet.subject_check(net)

text = "Mia laughed and turned to her brother. The kite climbed 6 metres."
motion.motion_find(text)                               # MotionFind[text]
# {'Motions': [['turned to her brother'], ['the kite climbed 6 metres']],
#  'Set aside': [{'Text': 'mia laughed', 'Reason': 'no motion words'}], 'Figures of speech': []}

motion.motion_find(text, subject_check=check)          # MotionFind[text, "SubjectCheck" -> SubjectCheckA]
# {'Motions': [['the kite climbed 6 metres']],
#  'Set aside': [{'Text': 'mia laughed', 'Reason': 'no motion words'},
#                {'Text': 'turned to her brother', 'Reason': 'about something else (subject check)'}],
#  'Figures of speech': []}

p = subjectnet.parts_of("mia turned to her brother")[0]
check(p), net.probabilities(subjectnet.feature_vector(p)[None, :])[0].round(4)
# ('other', array([0.0069, 0.9931]))

net.save("subjectnet.npz")                              # four plain arrays: W1, b1, W2, b2
```

What happened: without the check, "turned to her brother" was read as a turn of the object. With it, SubjectNet saw no words before the verb, so it looked at the end of the part before ("mia laughed"), the join "and", the verb "turned" and "to her brother" after it, and answered "other" with probability 0.993.

## 12. Messages you may see

| Message | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Wolfram: `SubjectCheckA` returned unevaluated | `SubjectNet.nb` has not been evaluated | evaluate `motion/MotionPhrases.nb`, then `nets/SubjectNet.nb` |
| Wolfram: `MotionSubject` undefined | an older `MotionPhrases.nb` | use the one in this repository, which has the `"SubjectCheck"` option |
| Python: `ModuleNotFoundError: ccn_nets` | not run from `python/` | `cd python`, or add it to `PYTHONPATH` |
| Python: `TypeError: string indices must be integers` from `motion_subject` | a string was passed | pass a part record, as `subjectnet.parts_of(sentence)` gives |
| A part "set aside: no motion words" | the part has no motion verb | not a SubjectNet decision |

## 13. Quick reference card

```
WOLFRAM                                           PYTHON  (cd python)
<< motion/MotionPhrases.nb, then SubjectNet.nb    from ccn_nets import motion, subjectnet
MotionFind[t, "SubjectCheck" -> SubjectCheckA]    motion.motion_find(t, subject_check=check)
MotionParse[t, "SubjectCheck" -> SubjectCheckB]   motion.motion_parse(t, subject_check=check)
MotionTransform[t, 1]                             motion.motion_transform(t, 1)
MotionSubject[part]                               motion.motion_subject(part)
                                                  net = subjectnet.run()["net"]
                                                  check = subjectnet.subject_check(net)
                                                  python3 -m ccn_nets.subjectnet
                                                  python3 -m unittest discover -s tests

NET  2048 hashed features → 32 ReLU → 2 softmax  ·  65,634 numbers
     Adam 0.005, L2 1e-4, batch 64, 12 passes, seed 1234
```

## 14. Files

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `nets/SubjectNet.nb` | the templates, the features, versions A and B, all five tests, the comparison |
| `nets/SubjectNet_as_matrices.nb` | the trained net written as matrices, typeset with `MatrixForm` |
| `nets/SubjectNetReport.md` | the report: our own net against Wolfram's |
| `motion/MotionPhrases.nb` | the reader, with the `"SubjectCheck"` option and `MotionSubject` |
| `python/ccn_nets/nn.py`, `motion.py`, `subjectnet.py` | the Python version |
| `python/tests/` | the tests against Wolfram's results |
| `nets/subjectnet/` | the Net Lab folder: `net.json`, `card.json`, `train/train.py`, `runs/`, `viz/` (`viewer-data.json`, `matrices.png`), `writeup.md`, this guide |

documents.name: SubjectNet: Write-up
documents.text:
## Aim

The motion reader (`MotionParse`) sometimes took a motion verb about something else as a motion of the object: "the camera holds on the kettle for a beat", "visitors often say the experience turns their sense of scale", "Mia laughed and turned to her brother". SubjectNet looks at each motion part and answers **object** (keep it) or **other** (set it aside).

## Data

The sentences are written from 19 templates, each with its own label, and read by the real motion reader, so the net sees parts exactly as they arrive. There are 2,000 training parts and 600 test parts; the test nouns, names and abstract words never appear in training, so the test shows whether the net learnt sentence shape rather than words. No conversational-construct labels anything.

## Design

Each part becomes a short list of features: the words before the verb (or, when there are none, the end of the part before it), how the part was joined to the one before, the verb, and the first words after it. The features are hashed into 2,048 slots of 0 or 1. Then 32 hidden units with ReLU, and a softmax over object and other: 65,634 numbers in all. It is trained with our own code (forward pass, backpropagation, Adam), written out in Wolfram and in Python, which agree to about 10⁻¹⁶.

## Results

On test sentences with unseen words, 99.5% are right, and 'other' is found with precision 1.0 and recall 0.99. Every one of the 47 paragraph parts is right, and 21 of 24 deliberately hard sentences. With SubjectNet, all 12 test paragraphs are read right step by step; without it, 9 of 12.

## Limits

The three hard sentences it gets wrong show its edges: "the lantern drifts upward 2 metres" (an unfamiliar subject with an unfamiliar verb), "my heart sank 2 times that day" (a figurative motion with a number), and "the cameraman slowly moves left" (a person who could be the moved thing). More templates of these kinds are the next step.

<!-- © Computational Classnotes · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 -->
# SubjectNet: our own net against Wolfram's, on one job

*24 November 2026. Measured on Wolfram 15.0.1 (Linux, a cloud evaluation kernel), not on your Mac, so the times are a guide only.*

## The job

Reading paragraphs, `MotionPhrases` sometimes took a motion verb about something else for a motion of the object. The three cases were:
- "the camera holds on the kettle for a beat";
- "visitors often say the experience turns their sense of scale";
- "Mia laughed and turned to her brother".

SubjectNet is a small neural net that looks at each motion part and answers **object** (keep it) or **other** (set it aside). It plugs in as one option:

```wolfram
MotionParse[text, "SubjectCheck" -> SubjectCheckA]    (* or SubjectCheckB *)
```

## Two versions, built the same way

| | Version A: our own | Version B: Wolfram's |
|---|---|---|
| The net | 2048 inputs → 32 hidden units (max(0, x)) → 2 outputs (softmax) | the same: `NetChain[{LinearLayer[32], Ramp, LinearLayer[2], SoftmaxLayer[]}]` |
| Forward pass, backpropagation, Adam | **written out in this notebook**, using only `Dot`, `Exp`, `Log`, `Total`, `Transpose`, `UnitStep` | `NetTrain` with `"ADAM"` |
| Wolfram neural-net functions used | **none** | `NetChain`, `NetTrain`, `NetDecoder` and the layers |
| Settings | learning rate 0.005, L2 10⁻⁴, batches of 64, 12 passes, seed 1234 | the same |
| Data and features | the same 2,000 training parts, the same features | the same |

The gradients in version A were checked against finite differences. The largest difference was **6.7 × 10⁻¹²**.

### Where the data came from

**No conversational-construct labelled anything, and no outside data was used.** The notebook writes the training sentences itself, from templates, and each template carries its own label:

- **19 templates.** For example, about the object: "the {thing} should {imperative}" and "to inspect the {thing}, {imperative}". About something else: "{name} {laughed} and turned to {her} {relation}", "{camera} holds on the {thing}" and "{the news} turned {his} {mood}".
- **Separate words for training and testing.** The test nouns, names, relations and abstract words (teapot, kite, sphere, gripper, Mia, brother, the experience, sense of scale…) never appear in training, so the test shows whether the net learnt sentence shape rather than words.
- **Read by the real code.** Every sentence goes through `MotionFind`, so the net sees motion parts exactly as `MotionParse` hands them over.
- **Size:** 2,000 training parts (1,328 object, 672 other) and 600 test parts (401 and 199). Writing the 2,000 takes 4.6 s.
- **Some overlap with the paragraphs:** a few words in the paragraph test are also in the training lists ("drone", "robot", "camera"), because they are ordinary words for this job.

### What the net sees

Each part becomes a list of short features, hashed into 2,048 slots of 0 or 1:
- the words before the motion verb ("o:the", "o:camera");
- when there are none, the last words of the part before it in the sentence ("p:mia", "p:laughed");
- how the part was joined to the one before it (and, comma, while, then);
- the verb itself;
- the first words after the verb ("a:to", "a:her", and the pair "a2:to_her").

## The algorithm of version A, in pseudocode

```
FORWARD(W1, b1, W2, b2, X):            -- X: a batch of feature vectors, one per row
    Z1 ← X·W1 + b1;  A1 ← max(0, Z1)
    P  ← softmax(A1·W2 + b2)           -- per row: exp(z − max z) / sum

BACKWARD(X, Y, P):                     -- Y: the right answers, one-hot; n rows
    dZ2 ← (P − Y) / n
    dW2 ← A1ᵀ·dZ2 + λ·W2;   db2 ← column sums of dZ2
    dZ1 ← (dZ2·W2ᵀ) × [Z1 > 0]
    dW1 ← Xᵀ·dZ1 + λ·W1;    db1 ← column sums of dZ1

TRAIN:
    W1, W2 ← random normal (He scaling), seed 1234;  b1, b2 ← 0;  m, v ← 0
    repeat 12 times: shuffle; for each batch of 64:
        t ← t + 1;  g ← BACKWARD(...)
        m ← 0.9·m + 0.1·g;   v ← 0.999·v + 0.001·g²
        θ ← θ − 0.005 · (m / (1 − 0.9ᵗ)) / (√(v / (1 − 0.999ᵗ)) + 10⁻⁸)

CHECK(part) = "object" or "other", whichever output of FORWARD is larger
```

## Results

| | Version A: our own | Version B: Wolfram's |
|---|---|---|
| Test 1: 600 template parts with unseen words | **100%** | **100%** |
| "Other" found (precision / recall), test 1 | 1.00 / 1.00 | 1.00 / 1.00 |
| Test 2: the 47 motion parts in the 12 paragraphs | **47 of 47** | **47 of 47** |
| Test 3: 24 parts from 23 harder sentences in new shapes | 21 of 24 | 21 of 24 |
| Test 4: paragraphs right step by step, with the check on | **12 of 12** (was 9 without it) | **12 of 12** |
| Test 5: the 557 phrase variants, with the check on | 546 (547 without it) | 546 |
| Training time | 1.0 s | 1.0 s |
| Time to check one part | **0.40 ms** | 0.86 ms |
| Numbers in the net | 65,634 | 65,634 |
| Code to build and train it | about 40 lines, all readable | about 5 lines |
| Wolfram neural-net functions used | none | NetChain, NetTrain and the layers |

**The two versions agreed on every single decision in every test.** With the same design, data and settings, writing the net ourselves cost nothing in accuracy. Ours was also twice as fast per part, because there is no net object to call.

### What each one got wrong

Both versions made exactly the same mistakes.

- **Test 3, three of 24:**
  - "The lantern drifts upward 2 metres" was set aside. "Lantern" was never seen, and "drifts" appears mostly in the camera templates ("the camera drifts across").
  - "My heart sank 2 times that day" was kept. This kind of figure of speech isn't in the templates.
  - "The cameraman slowly moves left" was kept. "Cameraman" was never seen; only "the camera" was.
  
  One sentence, "the detective circled back to the first clue", never reached the net, because the list of figures of speech had already set it aside.
- **Test 5, one new miss:** "about the x axis spin counterclockwise 270 degrees", a run-on variant with no comma. The words before "spin" ("about the x axis") look like a subject, so the part was set aside. With the comma ("about the x axis, spin…") it is read right.

### How far to trust these numbers

- **Test 1 is easy:** it uses the same templates with different words. It shows the net learnt sentence shape, not that it understands English.
- **Test 2 is real text,** but it has only three "other" parts.
- **Test 3 is the honest measure of generalisation:** 88% on shapes the templates never had. It is small (24 parts), and I wrote these sentences myself as a test, just as I wrote the paragraphs.
- **The way to improve it** is more templates, or real labelled parts from the motion reports, rather than a bigger net.

## Our own net against Wolfram's: beyond the numbers

| | Version A: our own | Version B: Wolfram's |
|---|---|---|
| Can be read and checked line by line | yes: every step is in the notebook, and the gradient check is included | the training is inside `NetTrain` |
| Runs elsewhere | the weights are four plain arrays: the same 10 lines of arithmetic run in Python or JavaScript | through ONNX export (draft 8 tested a Wolfram-to-Python ONNX round trip), or Wolfram only |
| Grows to bigger nets | each new kind of layer must be written out by hand, with its gradient | any layer Wolfram has (embeddings, attention, LSTM), with GPU training |
| Fits draft 8's "own nets" | yes, and the most portable | yes: the planned exchange through ONNX |

**A suggestion:** keep version A as the reference for small nets like this one, since it is transparent, tiny and portable. Use version B when a job needs layers we'd rather not write by hand. Either way, keep both versions trained on the same data, as here, so each checks the other.

## Files

- `nets/SubjectNet.nb`: the template data, the features, both versions, all five tests, and the comparison table. Evaluate it after `motion/MotionPhrases.nb` (its first cell loads that).
- `motion/MotionPhrases.nb`: the new `"SubjectCheck"` option and `MotionSubject`, which shows what a check sees of one part.

The notebook holds the code that was run for these numbers, arranged into cells; a few local names differ from the test runs. It hasn't yet been opened in Mathematica itself.

---

documents.text:
# The Python version

A complete Python version of the motion-phrase reader and of SubjectNet. Every neural-net piece is our own code: dense layers, ReLU, Tanh, Sigmoid, softmax, cross-entropy with L2, the forward pass, backpropagation, Adam, the initial weights and the gradient check. No neural-net library is used. NumPy holds the arrays and does their arithmetic (dot products, exp, log, sums), as `Dot`, `Exp` and `Total` do in the Wolfram version A.

It needs Python 3.9 or later and NumPy, and nothing else.

```
cd python
python3 -m ccn_nets.subjectnet              # make the data, train SubjectNet, run the four tests
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v    # the tests against Wolfram's results
```

## The files

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `ccn_nets/nn.py` | Our own neural-net code: `Net` (dense layers with an activation each and softmax at the end), `softmax_rows`, `cross_entropy`, `Net.forward`, `Net.gradients` (backpropagation), `Adam`, `train`, `gradient_check`, `Net.save` and `Net.load` |
| `ccn_nets/motion.py` | A port of `motion/MotionPhrases.nb`: tidying of dictated speech, steps and parts, the reading of each part, the subject records (`motion_subject`), `motion_find`, `motion_parse`, and `motion_transform`, which gives the pose as a 4 × 4 matrix |
| `ccn_nets/subjectnet.py` | A port of `nets/SubjectNet.nb`: the templates (training and test words kept apart), `make_data`, the features hashed into 2,048 slots, training, the subject check for the reader, and the four tests |
| `ccn_nets/data/subjectnet_tests.json` | The 12 paragraphs, their short phrases and the 24 hard sentences, taken from `SubjectNet.nb` |
| `ccn_nets/data/near_words.txt` | The 1,799 real English words within the spelling-correction distance of a motion word (see below) |
| `tools/NearWords.nb` | Remakes that list from Wolfram's dictionary |
| `tests/test_ccn_nets.py`, `tests/wolfram_reference.json` | The tests, and the Wolfram results they compare with |

## Using it

```python
from ccn_nets import motion, subjectnet
from ccn_nets.nn import Net, train

motion.motion_find("move along the path while spinning counterclokwise and move upwards")
motion.motion_transform("rise 4 while spinning counterclockwise then move right 3", 1)   # the pose at the end

net = subjectnet.run()["net"]                                    # train SubjectNet and print the tests
check = subjectnet.subject_check(net)
motion.motion_find("Mia laughed and turned to her brother. The kite climbed 6 metres.", subject_check=check)

net = Net([20, 8, 3], ["Tanh"]).initialise(seed=1)                # any small net: sizes, activations
history = train(net, x, y, epochs=12, batch_size=64, lr=0.005, l2=1e-4)   # x: rows of features, y: one-hot
net.save("net.npz")
```

## The same as the Wolfram version

These checks were run against Wolfram itself on 24 November 2026. The Wolfram results are kept in `tests/wolfram_reference.json`, so the comparison can be repeated without Wolfram.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| **Training arithmetic:** the same starting weights and batches as Wolfram's version A, five epochs | Losses and weights differ by about 10⁻¹⁶, the last bit of a floating-point number |
| **Feature hashing:** Python's CRC32 against `Hash[…, "CRC32"]` | Identical slots |
| **The reader:** 116 texts, namely the 12 paragraphs, their 12 short phrases, the 24 hard sentences, 60 template sentences and 8 sentences with dictation slips | Identical records, motion parts and reasons for setting parts aside, in every text |
| **The poses:** the 12 short phrases at times 1 and 0.37, and the 12 paragraphs at time 1 | The largest difference is 5 × 10⁻¹⁰, the rounding of the Wolfram values |
| **Gradient checks** | 1.7 × 10⁻¹¹ (ReLU), 1.1 × 10⁻¹¹ (Tanh, Sigmoid and linear layers) |

## SubjectNet: Python and Wolfram compared

| | Python (our own code) | Wolfram A (our own code) | Wolfram B (NetTrain) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weights | 65,634 | 65,634 | 65,634 |
| Training time | 0.8 s | 1.0 s | 1.0 s |
| Test 1: templates with unseen words | 99.5% | 100% | 100% |
| Test 2: paragraph parts | 47 of 47 | 47 of 47 | 47 of 47 |
| Test 3: hard sentences | 21 of 24 | 21 of 24 | 21 of 24 |
| Test 4: paragraphs right step by step | 12 of 12 (9 without the check) | 12 of 12 | 12 of 12 |
| Time to check one part | 0.03 ms | 0.40 ms | 0.86 ms |

Test 3 goes wrong on the same three sentences in all three: the lantern, the heart and the cameraman.

Test 1 differs slightly because Python's random numbers are not Wolfram's. The template sentences, and so the training and test data, are therefore different draws from the same templates. In this draw, Python's net called three of the 221 "other" parts "object".

## The word list

When a word is misspelt, the reader replaces it with the nearest motion word ("counterclokwise" becomes "counterclockwise"), but it never changes a real word. Wolfram decides what counts as a real word with `DictionaryWordQ`, and Python has no dictionary of its own.

Only the real words that lie within one or two letters of a motion word could ever be wrongly corrected, so `tools/NearWords.nb` lists exactly those from Wolfram's dictionary. "fails" is one: it is never turned into "falls". This reproduces Wolfram's behaviour exactly, with no extra package.

Evaluate `tools/NearWords.nb` again whenever the motion vocabulary changes.

## Not yet

- ONNX export, so that a net trained here can be read by Wolfram, and the other way round, as draft 8 describes.
- Branching nets and dropout in our own code.

The net diagram editor (`editor/net-diagram-editor.html`) writes a Python script that uses this code: choose **Python** under Language.

By Dara O Shayda and Hikari Noor Hoshino (星野ヌール)
